flashcards.q: Why does applying a metadata filter to an ANN index break both naive strategies?
flashcards.a: Every ANN index (HNSW, IVF) is built assuming any indexed vector is a valid target. Pre-filtering restricts to a subset with no ANN index built over it, degenerating toward brute force. Post-filtering discards non-matches after search, which can silently under-return since the greedy search never routed toward the filter-valid region.

flashcards.q: Give the concrete arithmetic of post-filter under-return.
flashcards.a: A filter matching ~10% of the corpus with a default beam width like ef_search=40 retrieves on average only ~4 filter-valid candidates by chance -- well short of a k=10 request, even though far more valid matches exist elsewhere in the graph.

flashcards.q: Define cardinality and selectivity, and explain why high-cardinality filters are the expensive case.
flashcards.a: Cardinality = number of distinct values a field can take. Selectivity = fraction of corpus a specific value matches. High-cardinality fields (tenant_id, millions of values) produce high selectivity per value, which is worst for both strategies: pre-filter scans a small unindexed subset, post-filter suffers the most severe under-return.

flashcards.q: State the non-negotiable rule for ACL-aware filtering.
flashcards.a: The ACL filter must be applied IN the retrieval query itself, never as a post-retrieval check. Retrieve-then-discard means unauthorized data may already be logged, cached, briefly in a response payload, or exposed via a timing/count side-channel before the discard runs.

flashcards.q: What does Weaviate's ACORN do to fix filtered search?
flashcards.a: Multi-hop graph expansion so the search radius covers enough of the graph to find filter-valid neighbors regardless of selectivity. As of v1.34 it automatically chooses between multi-hop exploration (selective filters), relaxed broader traversal (broad filters), or flat brute-force scan (tiny result sets).

flashcards.q: What does Pinecone do by default for filtered search, and what's the risk?
flashcards.a: Merges metadata and vector index into one structure and defaults to post-filtering -- fast on average but carries the classic under-return risk on highly selective filters unless the caller oversamples.

flashcards.q: What is oversampling as a post-filter mitigation, and why is it not a fix?
flashcards.a: Request k*factor candidates (e.g. k=10 as k1=50-100), then filter down. Reduces but doesn't eliminate under-return since the search still isn't routing toward the filter-valid region deliberately -- a selective enough filter can still under-return, and it costs proportionally more compute.

flashcards.q: Compare shared index with a tenant_id metadata field vs. separate collection per tenant.
flashcards.a: Shared index: simplest to operate, one schema, but inherits all pre/post-filter tradeoffs scaled by tenant-size skew. Separate collection: isolates performance/data completely, no filter-vs-graph reconciliation, at the cost of N indexes to build/monitor/reindex.

flashcards.q: For a tenant-size distribution from 100 to 5 million documents, what's the right multi-tenancy strategy?
flashcards.a: Tiered: smallest tenants use brute-force/in-memory search (trivially fast, sidesteps the filtered-ANN problem); mid-size tenants share a filtered index with a filter-aware strategy; largest tenants get dedicated physical index isolation for both performance and blast-radius isolation.

flashcards.q: Compare RBAC and ABAC for retrieval filtering.
flashcards.a: RBAC: permissions on roles -- simple, coarse-grained. ABAC: permissions computed from user+resource+context attributes (e.g. department match AND clearance >= sensitivity) -- finer-grained, more complex to evaluate. Production systems typically layer both rather than choosing either/or.

flashcards.q: Why is denormalizing metadata onto chunk records the right call, and what risk does it carry?
flashcards.a: Vector databases generally don't support efficient joins, and a per-query round-trip to a separate permissions store adds latency to every retrieval call. Risk: the denormalized copy can drift out of sync with the source of truth (e.g. an ACL change) until the next sync/backfill -- requires explicit staleness monitoring, especially for ACLs.

flashcards.q: When does schema evolution require a full reindex, and when doesn't it?
flashcards.a: Adding a new filterable field is typically a metadata backfill only -- the vector is unaffected, no re-embedding needed. Changing an existing field's type/semantics (boolean to enum) requires auditing every dependent code path and a transitional sentinel state during rollout, since partial migration can produce inconsistent filtering.

Continues traversing further into the graph (deeper beam, more candidates) until enough filter-valid results are found or a scan-depth limit is hit -- a filter-aware mitigation for moderate-selectivity filters.
